s0001: Estimate what fraction of a circle a spinner sector takes up and find the expected number of outcomes over many spins
s0002: Work out what part of the circle the sector takes up (using its angle), then multiply the number of spins by that fraction.
s0003: Malika made the spinner shown for a new game. If the spinner is spun 480 times, about how many times would you expect it to stop on the “Green” sector?
s0008: The “Green” sector is half of a right angle: $45°$
s0009: In the picture, the green sector is half the size of the blue sector, which is a right angle, so it is forty-five degrees.
s0010: Forty-five degrees is one eighth of the whole circle.
s0011: One eighth of four hundred eighty is sixty.
s0014: A student who chose A took the green sector to be a right angle (a quarter of the circle): $480 : 4 = 120$.
s0015: A student who chose B wrongly estimated the sector as one sixth of the circle: $480 : 6 = 80$.
s0016: A student who chose D took the sector to be very small, one twelfth of the circle: $480 : 12 = 40$.
s0017: Compare the green sector with the blue right-angle sector next to it.
s0018: Aziz is going to spin the spinner shown 900 times. About how many times would you expect it to stop on the “Pink” sector?
s0021: “White” is a half circle ($180°$); “Yellow” is 2 times as big as “Pink”
s0022: The white sector is half of the circle; in the other half, the yellow sector is twice as big as the pink one.
s0024: So if the half circle is split into three equal parts, the pink sector is one of them: sixty degrees.
s0025: Sixty degrees is one sixth of the circle.
s0026: One sixth of nine hundred is one hundred fifty.
s0029: A student who chose A underestimated the sector as one ninth of the circle: $900 : 9 = 100$.
s0030: A student who chose C took the pink sector to be a right angle (a quarter circle): $900 : 4 = 225$.
s0031: A student who chose D confused the pink sector with the yellow sector (120°, one third of the circle): $900 : 3 = 300$.
s0032: Start by finding what part of the circle the white sector is.
s0033: Write two inequalities from the positions of balance scales and find a value that satisfies both
s0034: Write an inequality for each scale (the heavier pan goes down). When there are several pieces, divide the inequality by the number of pieces, then choose the value that fits both conditions.
s0035:
Aziz has 4 iron pieces that all have the same mass.
When he weighed one piece against a 15 g weight, the pan with the piece went up (top scale in the picture).
When he weighed all four pieces against a 52 g weight, the pan with the pieces went down (bottom scale).
Which of the following could be the mass of one piece?
s0037: On the first scale, the pan with the piece went up, so the piece is lighter than fifteen grams.
s0039: On the second scale, the four pieces are heavier than fifty-two grams.
s0040: Fifty-two divided by four is thirteen: one piece is heavier than thirteen grams.
s0041: The only option between thirteen and fifteen is fourteen.
s0043: A student who chose A calculated $52 : 4 = 13$ but did not take into account that the pieces are heavier than the weight, so each must be more than 13 g.
s0044: A student who chose C thought the first scale was balanced; in fact, the piece is lighter than 15 g.
s0045: A student who chose D read the first scale the wrong way around: the pan with the piece going up means the piece is lighter.
s0046: Write a separate inequality for each scale and find a number that fits both.
s0047:
A farmer has 5 sacks of flour that all have the same mass.
When one sack was weighed against a 9 kg weight, the pan with the sack went down (top scale in the picture).
When all five sacks were weighed against a 55 kg weight, the pan with the sacks went up (bottom scale).
Which of the following could be the mass of one sack?
s0056: On the first scale, the pan with the sack went down, so the sack is heavier than nine kilograms.
s0058: On the second scale, the five sacks are lighter than fifty-five kilograms.
s0060: Fifty-five divided by five is eleven: one sack is lighter than eleven kilograms.
s0062: The option between nine and eleven is ten.
s0064: A student who chose A read the first scale the wrong way around: the pan with the sack going down means the sack is heavier.
s0065: A student who chose B thought the first scale was balanced; in fact, the sack is heavier than 9 kg.
s0066: A student who chose D found $55 : 5 = 11$ but did not take into account that the sacks are lighter than the weight, so each must be less than 11 kg.
s0067: The heavier pan goes down: for each scale, write a “greater than” or “less than” inequality.
s0068: Read the time that matches a given value from a cumulative line graph
s0069: Find the value you need on the vertical axis, go across horizontally to the solid line, then go down and read the time.
s0070:
The solid line on the graph shows the total number of loaves made at the “Bereke” bakery during one day. The dashed line shows what the total would be if the loaves were made at a steady rate.
At what time had a total of 240 loaves been made?
s0075: We find the two hundred forty mark on the vertical axis.
s0076: From 240, go across to the solid line
s0077: From there we go right until we reach the solid line, not the dashed line!
s0079: Going down from the point where they meet, we get ten o'clock.
s0081: A student who chose A took the value at 9:00 (180) as close to 240 and did not read the graph carefully.
s0082: A student who chose C used the dashed line instead of the solid line: it reaches 240 at 11:00.
s0083: A student who chose D took a value already past 240 (300 at 12:00) or miscounted the grid columns.
s0084: Look at the solid line, which shows the actual result, not the dashed line.

s0089: We find the two hundred kilogram mark on the vertical axis.
s0090: From 200, go across to the solid line
s0091: From there we go right until we reach the solid line.
s0093: Going down from the point where they meet, we get eleven o'clock.

s0096: A student who chose C used the dashed line: it reaches 200 kg at 12:00.

s0099: Read the total amount and time from a cumulative graph and calculate the average rate per hour
s0100: Find the total amount from the last point of the graph and the total number of hours from the horizontal axis, then divide the total amount by the number of hours.
s0101:
The solid line on the graph shows the total number of loaves made at the “Bereke” bakery during one day. The dashed line shows what the total would be if the loaves were made at a steady rate.
On average, how many loaves did the bakery make per hour that day?
s0104: The last point of the graph is four hundred eighty, at fifteen hundred hours.
s0106: Work went on from seven to fifteen hundred hours, which is eight hours.
s0107: We divide four hundred eighty by eight: sixty.
s0109: On average, sixty loaves were made per hour.
s0110: Typical mistakes: writing the total (480) as the average, or miscounting the hours and dividing by 9 (there are 9 time marks but only 8 intervals).
s0111: Average rate = total amount : total time; count the hours by intervals, not by marks.
s0112:
The solid line on the graph shows the total mass of grapes picked in the Nilufar family's vineyard during one day. The dashed line shows what the total mass would be if the grapes were picked at a steady rate.
On average, how many kilograms of grapes were picked per hour that day?
s0115: The last point of the graph is three hundred kilograms, at fourteen hundred hours.
s0117: The picking went on from eight to fourteen hundred hours, which is six hours.
s0118: We divide three hundred by six: fifty.
s0120: On average, fifty kilograms of grapes were picked per hour.
s0121: Typical mistakes: writing the total mass (300) as the average, or counting the time marks and dividing by 7.
s0122: Work out how many hours the graph covers by counting the intervals.
s0123: Find the steepest part of a cumulative graph to identify the hour with the greatest output
s0124: For each hour, find the change in the total (next value − previous value), or find the part of the graph that rises most steeply.
s0125:
The solid line on the graph shows the total number of loaves made at the “Bereke” bakery during one day. The dashed line shows what the total would be if the loaves were made at a steady rate.
During which one hour were the most loaves made?
s0131: For each hour, we subtract the previous value from the next one.
s0132: The biggest increase is between twelve and thirteen hundred hours: one hundred twenty loaves.
s0133: The steepest part of the graph is here too
s0134: On the graph, this part also rises most steeply.
s0136: A student who chose A saw the increase of 100 in the first hour but did not check the later increase of 120.
s0137: A student who chose B chose a part where the graph is almost flat: only 20 loaves were made in that hour.
s0138: A student who chose D thought the highest point of the graph showed the hour with the most output; in fact, it is the total, not the amount for one hour.
s0139: Look for the part that rises most steeply, not the highest point.
